Improving neural network performance for solving quantum sign structure

Preprint: APS/123-QED
Xiaowei Ou Email: xiaowei.ou@yale.edu Affiliation: Department of Physics, Yale University, New Haven, Connecticut 06520, USA Affiliation: Energy Sciences Institute, Yale University, West Haven, Connecticut 06516, USA    Tianshu Huang Affiliation: Energy Sciences Institute, Yale University, West Haven, Connecticut 06516, USA Affiliation: Department of Applied Physics, Yale University, New Haven, Connecticut 06520, USA    Vidvuds Ozoliņš Email: vidvuds.ozolins@yale.edu Affiliation: Energy Sciences Institute, Yale University, West Haven, Connecticut 06516, USA Affiliation: Department of Applied Physics, Yale University, New Haven, Connecticut 06520, USA
August 24, 2026
Abstract

Neural quantum states have emerged as a widely used approach to the numerical study of the ground states of non-stoquastic Hamiltonians. However, existing approaches often rely on a priori knowledge of the sign structure or require a separately pre-trained phase network. We introduce a modified stochastic reconfiguration method that effectively uses differing imaginary time steps to evolve the amplitude and phase. Using a larger time step for phase optimization, this method enables a simultaneous and efficient training of phase and amplitude neural networks. The efficacy of our method is demonstrated on the Heisenberg J1−J2J_{1}-J_{2} model.

I Introduction

Finding ground states in strongly interacting many-body systems is an important problem due to its connection to many intriguing phenomena in condensed matter physics, such as quantum spin liquids [1, 2], high TcT_{c} superconductors [3], and topological insulators [4]. However, analytical solutions are rarely possible [5], and the exponential growth of the Hilbert space with respect to the system size presents challenges for numerical studies.

Many numerical methods have been developed to address specific classes of problems efficiently, but with characteristic limitations. For instance, exact diagonalization methods [6, 7] are applicable only to small system sizes. Quantum Monte Carlo [8, 9] encounters difficulties in frustrated and fermionic systems due to the infamous sign problem [10]. The density matrix renormalization group [11] is very successful in low-dimensional systems, but it becomes cumbersome in higher dimensions. Complementary to all these are variational approaches, which aim to efficiently parametrize the physically relevant part of the Hilbert space. Various methods lie in this category, such as Jastrow- and Gutzwiller-projected wave functions [12, 13], tensor network states [14, 15], projected entangled pair states [16, 17] and, most recently, neural quantum states (NQS).

Neural quantum states were first introduced using restricted Boltzmann machine as a practical wave-function Ansatz [18]. Since then, this neural network architecture has been widely studied [19, 20, 21, 22]. Apart from the restricted Boltzmann machine, a variety of other architectures have been explored, including fully connected neural networks [23], convolutional neural networks [23, 24, 25, 26, 27], recurrent neural networks [28], autoregressive models [29], transformer neural networks [30], and various neural network inspired Ansäzte with physical information [31, 32, 33, 34, 35, 36]. These architectures have been used to study ground-state and the lowest excited-state [37] properties in strongly correlated one- (1D) and two-dimensional (2D) systems.

Neural quantum states have several advantages over other variational Ansäzte. First, because of the universal approximation theorems, a neural network with a sufficient number of parameters can represent any function [38], hence in principle it does not have any variational bias. Second, neural quantum states can be easily generalized to higher-dimensional systems and larger system sizes [26]. Third, NQS requires sub-exponential number of parameters to encode volume-law entangled states [39, 40, 21, 41].

In spite of all these advantages, many challenges remain when using neural quantum states. For instance, representing the non-trivial sign structure in frustrated and fermionic systems is still a difficult problem [42, 43, 44, 45, 46, 47]. Furthermore, due to a rugged landscape in the parameter space [48], optimization of neural network parameters is often difficult and requires substantial computational resources.

In this work, to alleviate the problem of optimizing non-trivial sign structure, we propose an improved stochastic reconfiguration method (SR), which introduces different learning rates for the optimization of the amplitude and phase of the wave function. By employing a faster learning rate for the phase, our proposed method effectively balances the contributions from the phase and amplitude to the gradients in the network parameter space. This algorithm is tested on the paradigmatic Heisenberg J1−J2J_{1}-J_{2} model on a 6×66\times 6 square lattice, and they are shown to perform reliably and efficiently.

II Neural quantum states

In a spin lattice system with N sites, a quantum state can be expanded as |ψ⟩=∑σψθ​(σ)​|σ⟩\ket{\psi}=\sum_{\sigma}\psi_{\theta}(\sigma)\ket{\sigma}, where σ=(σ1,σ2,…,σN)\sigma=(\sigma_{1},\sigma_{2},...,\sigma_{N}) are {S^iz}\{\hat{S}_{i}^{z}\} eigenstates spanning the Hilbert space of the spin configurations, and θ\theta denotes the vector of variational parameters. In neural quantum states, the Ansatz function ψθ​(σ)\psi_{\theta}(\sigma) is given by an artificial neural network, where the input is a basis spin configuration σ\sigma, encoded by a 2D matrix with values +1+1 (−1)(-1) denoting up (down) spin states. It is common practice to have the neural network output the logarithm of the wave function, so that it can accurately capture coefficients over multiple orders of magnitude. In this work we use

ln⁡[ψθ​(σ)]=Aθ​(σ)+i​ϕθ​(σ),\ln[\psi_{\theta}(\sigma)]=A_{\theta}(\sigma)+i\phi_{\theta}(\sigma), (1)

where Aθ​(σ)A_{\theta}(\sigma) and ϕθ​(σ)\phi_{\theta}(\sigma) are outputs from two independent real-valued neural networks. It has been noted that the most accurate results are usually obtained with networks that do not make such a separation but allow the flow of information between the phase and amplitude. Our proposed methods in Sections IV remain applicable to these more complex architectures and they can support both real-valued and complex-valued network parameters.

Figure 1 shows the neural network architecture. For Aθ​(σ)A_{\theta}(\sigma), the 2D configuration first passes through a convolutional layer with 64 6×66\times 6 kernels. We then take absolute value for each element, followed by taking the maximum value for each site across the 64 kernels, and then sum over all sites to get the output. This can be formally written as

Aθ​(σ)=∑i​jmaxc⁡|∑l​mwl,mc​σi+l,j+m+bc|,A_{\theta}(\sigma)=\sum_{ij}\max_{c}\left|\sum_{lm}w_{l,m}^{c}\sigma_{i+l,j+m}+b^{c}\right|, (2)

where (i,j)(i,j) index lattice sites in the input configuration σ\sigma, cc is the channel number, and (l,m)(l,m) index kernel sites after the convolution. Tensors wcw^{c} are the kernel weights, and bcb^{c} are biases.

For the phase ϕθ​(σ)\phi_{\theta}(\sigma) we use three fully-connected layers each followed by ReLU (ReLU​(x)=max⁡(0,x)\text{ReLU}(x)=\max(0,x)), except after the last layer. The number of neurons in the hidden layers are both 8, and the number of neurons in the output layer is 1. In total, our neural networks have 2745 real-valued parameters. We use 2000 Monte Carlo samples and optimize the network using Nesterov’s accelerated gradient method [5] with momentum coefficient μ=0.5\mu=0.5 and learning rate of 0.040.04. Our work uses a simple architecture with reasonably good but not the best possible performance in order to focus on the method for optimizing neural quantum states.

We further enforce the symmetry of the C4​vC_{4v} point group. Since the ground state is fully symmetric with a total wave vector 𝐤=𝟎\mathbf{k}=\mathbf{0} [50], we use the characters of the A1A_{1} irreducible representation. In the case where the group representation A1A_{1} is one-dimensional, the symmetrized wave function can be written as

ψθ​(σ)=1|G|​∑g∈Gχ⁡(g)​ψθ​(g^​σ)\psi_{\theta}(\sigma)=\frac{1}{|G|}\sum_{g\in G}\chi(g)\psi_{\theta}(\hat{g}\sigma) (3)

where gg is a group element, χ⁡(g)\chi(g) is the character corresponding to gg, and GG is the point group C4​vC_{4v}. Translational symmetry is automatically enforced for the amplitude by the convolutional layer in the net.

We have also tested an approach that uses explicitly symmetrized basis functions instead of |σ⟩\ket{\sigma}. This method may prove particularly useful when one is interested in obtaining states of given symmetry at 𝐤≠𝟎\mathbf{k}\neq\mathbf{0}. It is described in Appendix A, and its performance is found to be very similar to Eq. (3).

III Stochastic Reconfiguration

The Wick-rotated Schrödinger equation governs imaginary time evolution according to

∂|ψ⁡(τ)⟩∂τ=−(ℋ−E)​|ψ⁡(τ)⟩,\frac{\partial\ket{\psi(\tau)}}{\partial\tau}=-(\mathcal{H}-E)\ket{\psi(\tau)}, (4)

where E=⟨ψ⁡(τ)|​ℋ​|ψ⁡(τ)⟩E=\bra{\psi(\tau)}\mathcal{H}\ket{\psi(\tau)} is the energy expectation value, introduced to preserve the normalization constraint ⟨ψ|ψ⟩=1\innerproduct{\psi}{\psi}=1. Numerically, EE is estimated as a Monte Carlo average over NsN_{s} samples drawn from the probability distribution |ψθ​(σ)|2|\psi_{\theta}(\sigma)|^{2}: E=⟨Eloc​(σ)⟩E=\langle E_{\text{loc}}(\sigma)\rangle. Here, Eloc​(σ)=∑σ′ℋσ​σ′​ψθ​(σ′)ψθ​(σ)E_{\text{loc}}(\sigma)=\sum_{\sigma^{\prime}}\mathcal{H}_{\sigma\sigma^{\prime}}\frac{\psi_{\theta}(\sigma^{\prime})}{\psi_{\theta}(\sigma)} represents the local energy, and the wave function ψθ​(σ)\psi_{\theta}(\sigma) is parameterized by NpN_{p} variational parameters θ\theta.

The imaginary time evolution induces an infinitesimal change in the wave function components

δ​ψσ=−ψσ​(Eloc​(σ)−E)​δ​τ.\delta\psi_{\sigma}=-\psi_{\sigma}\left(E_{\text{loc}}(\sigma)-E\right)\delta\tau. (5)

On the other hand, parameter variations generate changes through ∑k∂ψσ∂θk​δ​θk\sum_{k}\frac{\partial\psi_{\sigma}}{\partial\theta_{k}}\delta\theta_{k}. Since we require this change to lie within the tangent space of |ψ⟩\ket{\psi}, we apply the projection operator P^=𝕀−|ψ⟩​⟨ψ|\hat{P}=\mathbb{I}-\ket{\psi}\bra{\psi}, yielding

δ​ψσ′=ψσ​∑k(Oσ​k−⟨Oσ​k⟩)​δ​θk,\displaystyle\delta\psi^{\prime}_{\sigma}=\psi_{\sigma}\sum_{k}(O_{\sigma k}-\langle O_{\sigma k}\rangle)\delta\theta_{k}, (6)

where Oσ​k=∂ln⁡ψθ​(σ)∂θkO_{\sigma k}=\frac{\partial\ln\psi_{\theta}(\sigma)}{\partial\theta_{k}} is the logarithmic derivative of the wave function.

To determine the optimal parameter updates δ​θk\delta\theta_{k}, we minimize the distance between the imaginary-time-evolved state change δ​ψ\delta\psi and the variational state change δ​ψ′\delta\psi^{\prime}

d2=∥δ​ψ′−δ​ψ∥2\displaystyle d^{2}=\lVert\delta\psi^{\prime}-\delta\psi\rVert^{2} =∥O¯​δ​θ−ϵ¯∥2,\displaystyle=\lVert\bar{O}\delta\theta-\bar{\epsilon}\rVert^{2}, (7)

where we have defined the NsN_{s}-dimensional vector ϵ¯σ=−δτ(Eloc(σ)−E)/Ns\bar{\epsilon}_{\sigma}=-\delta\tau(E_{\text{loc}}(\sigma)-E)/\sqrt{N_{s}}, and the Ns×NpN_{s}\times N_{p} matrix O¯σ​k=(Oσ​k−⟨Oσ​k⟩)/Ns\bar{O}_{\sigma k}=(O_{\sigma k}-\langle O_{\sigma k}\rangle)/\sqrt{N_{s}}.

Since the matrix O¯\bar{O} is typically ill-conditioned or singular, Tikhonov regularization is employed to stabilize the optimization, which leads to the following Lagrangian:

ℒSR=β​∥δ​θ∥2+∥O¯​δ​θ−ϵ¯∥2.\mathcal{L}_{\text{SR}}=\beta\lVert\delta\theta\rVert^{2}+\lVert\bar{O}\delta\theta-\bar{\epsilon}\rVert^{2}. (8)

Setting ∂ℒS​R/∂(δ​θ†)=0\partial\mathcal{L}_{SR}/\partial(\delta\theta^{\dagger})=0 gives the parameter update

δ​θ=(O¯†​O¯+β​𝕀)−1​O¯†​ϵ¯.\delta\theta=(\bar{O}^{\dagger}\bar{O}+\beta\mathbb{I})^{-1}\bar{O}^{\dagger}\bar{\epsilon}. (9)

This formula, which we refer to as stochastic reconfiguration, requires inverting an Np×NpN_{p}\times N_{p} matrix. For most modern NQS architectures with a large number of parameters one has Ns≪NpN_{s}\ll N_{p}, and the Woodbury matrix identity [51] provides a computationally more efficient alternative:

δ​θ=O¯†​(O¯​O¯†+β​𝕀)−1​ϵ¯.\delta\theta=\bar{O}^{\dagger}(\bar{O}\bar{O}^{\dagger}+\beta\mathbb{I})^{-1}\bar{\epsilon}. (10)

This so-called MinSR formula was first proposed by Chen and Heyl [52] and only requires inverting a much smaller Ns×NsN_{s}\times N_{s} matrix. Chen and Heyl derived the MinSR method using the following Lagrangian:

ℒMinSR=∥δ​θ∥2+(δ​θ†​O¯†−ϵ¯†)​μ,\mathcal{L}_{\text{MinSR}}=\lVert\delta\theta\rVert^{2}+(\delta\theta^{\dagger}\bar{O}^{\dagger}-\bar{\epsilon}^{\dagger})\mu, (11)

where μ\mu is the Lagrangian multiplier. The solution is δ​θ=O¯†​(O¯​O¯†)−1​ϵ¯\delta\theta=\bar{O}^{\dagger}(\bar{O}\bar{O}^{\dagger})^{-1}\bar{\epsilon}. In Ref. [52] regularization is introduced as a numerical stabilization step to arrive at Eq. (10). We note that in real computation, the constraint O¯​δ​θ=ϵ¯\bar{O}\delta\theta=\bar{\epsilon} cannot always be satisfied due to the approximate nature of the NQS, especially when approaching the true ground state. To account for this, we incorporate a residue term Δ\Delta into the constraint, leading to the modified Lagrangian:

ℒMinSR′=β​∥δ​θ∥2+(δ​θ†​O¯†−ϵ¯†−Δ†)​μ+∥Δ∥2.\mathcal{L}_{\text{MinSR}}^{\prime}=\beta\lVert\delta\theta\rVert^{2}+(\delta\theta^{\dagger}\bar{O}^{\dagger}-\bar{\epsilon}^{\dagger}-\Delta^{\dagger})\mu+\lVert\Delta\rVert^{2}. (12)

By minimizing this Lagrangian with respect to δ​θ\delta\theta and Δ\Delta (see the Supplementary Material), we naturally recover the regularized solution given in Eq. (10), providing an alternative justification for Tikhonov regularization in the MinSR framework.

IV Time-step adjusted optimization

The stochastic reconfiguration method faces challenges when training log-amplitude and phase networks simultaneously, particularly for systems with unknown sign structure, such as frustrated and fermionic systems. The faster changes of log-amplitude affect the Markov chain greatly, impeding the phase network’s ability to converge to a correct sign structure.

To illustrate the issue, consider a minimal example with two basis states, |ψ⟩=(ψ1,ψ2)T\ket{\psi}=(\psi_{1},\psi_{2})^{T}, where ψ1\psi_{1} and ψ2\psi_{2} are real-valued for the ground state. The energy expectation value is

E=h11​ψ12+h22​ψ22+(h12+h21)​ψ1​ψ2.E=h_{11}\psi_{1}^{2}+h_{22}\psi_{2}^{2}+(h_{12}+h_{21})\psi_{1}\psi_{2}. (13)

In the Heisenberg model, off-diagonal elements h12=h21≥0h_{12}=h_{21}\geq 0 require ψ1​ψ2≤0\psi_{1}\psi_{2}\leq 0 for energy minimization. However, if the phase network fails to predict the correct signs (yielding ψ1​ψ2≥0\psi_{1}\psi_{2}\geq 0), the log-amplitude network aggressively suppresses either |ψ1||\psi_{1}| or |ψ2||\psi_{2}| to eliminate the positive cross term. This biases the Markov chain toward configurations with the smallest diagonal energy hi​ih_{ii}, preventing exploration of the true ground state. Existing approaches for the two-dimensional Heisenberg J1−J2J_{1}-J_{2} model prioritize phase training [46] or incorporate specific rules into the Ansatz [24, 42] to address this issue.

To balance the training speeds of log-amplitude and phase networks, we can decouple the imaginary time evolution for amplitude and phase by advancing them at different rates. Using ψσ=Aσ​ei​ϕσ\psi_{\sigma}=A_{\sigma}e^{i\phi_{\sigma}}, we can rewrite Eq. (4) as

1Aσ​∂Aσ∂τ\displaystyle\frac{1}{A_{\sigma}}\frac{\partial A_{\sigma}}{\partial\tau} =−Re[Eloc​(σ)−E],\displaystyle=-\real\left[E_{\text{loc}}(\sigma)-E\right], (14)
∂ϕσ∂τ\displaystyle\frac{\partial\phi_{\sigma}}{\partial\tau} =−Im[Eloc​(σ)−E].\displaystyle=-\imaginary\left[E_{\text{loc}}(\sigma)-E\right]. (15)

The amplitude step δ​τA\delta\tau_{A} is limited by the nonlinearity implicit in the Monte Carlo average on the r.h.s. of Eq. (14) which requires one to resample the Markov chain upon large changes in AσA_{\sigma}. In contrast, the phase time step δ​τϕ\delta\tau_{\phi} can be larger, as advancing the phase using Eq. (15) does not affect the Monte Carlo sampling distribution,

Aσ(n+1)\displaystyle A_{\sigma}^{(n+1)} =Aσ(n)+δ​τA​∂Aσ∂τ,\displaystyle=A_{\sigma}^{(n)}+\delta\tau_{A}\frac{\partial A_{\sigma}}{\partial\tau}, (16)
ϕσ(n+1)\displaystyle\phi_{\sigma}^{(n+1)} =ϕσ(n)+δ​τϕ​∂ϕσ∂τ,\displaystyle=\phi_{\sigma}^{(n)}+\delta\tau_{\phi}\frac{\partial\phi_{\sigma}}{\partial\tau}, (17)

where δ​τA≤δ​τϕ\delta\tau_{A}\leq\delta\tau_{\phi}. This leads to the change in the wave function:

δ​ψσ\displaystyle\delta\psi_{\sigma} =ψσ​(1Aσ​∂Aσ∂τ​δ​τA+i​∂ϕσ∂τ​δ​τϕ).\displaystyle=\psi_{\sigma}\left(\frac{1}{A_{\sigma}}\frac{\partial A_{\sigma}}{\partial\tau}\delta\tau_{A}+i\frac{\partial\phi_{\sigma}}{\partial\tau}\delta\tau_{\phi}\right). (18)

As detailed in the Supplementary Material, the distance between δ​ψ′\delta\psi^{\prime} and δ​ψ\delta\psi is given by

d2=∥δ​ψ′−δ​ψ∥2=‖O¯​δ​θ−ϵ~‖2,d^{2}=\lVert\delta\psi^{\prime}-\delta\psi\rVert^{2}=||\bar{O}\delta\theta-\tilde{\epsilon}||^{2}, (19)

where ϵ~=Reϵ¯+miImϵ¯\tilde{\epsilon}=\real\bar{\epsilon}+mi\imaginary\bar{\epsilon} is a modified vector and m=δ​τϕδ​τA≥1m=\frac{\delta\tau_{\phi}}{\delta\tau_{A}}\geq 1 is the step size ratio. Minimizing this modified distance, we obtain the following parameter update rules:

SR: δθ\displaystyle\text{SR: }\delta\theta =(O¯†​O¯+β​𝕀)−1​O¯†​ϵ~,\displaystyle=(\bar{O}^{\dagger}\bar{O}+\beta\mathbb{I})^{-1}\bar{O}^{\dagger}\tilde{\epsilon}, (20)
MinSR: δθ\displaystyle\text{MinSR: }\delta\theta =O¯†​(O¯​O¯†+β​𝕀)−1​ϵ~.\displaystyle=\bar{O}^{\dagger}(\bar{O}\bar{O}^{\dagger}+\beta\mathbb{I})^{-1}\tilde{\epsilon}. (21)

This modification effectively slows the updates to the log-amplitude relative to the phase, which is crucial for learning unknown sign structure in challenging systems. Mathematically, Eq. (20) and Eq. (21) are equivalent. Both (O¯†​O¯+β​𝕀)(\bar{O}^{\dagger}\bar{O}+\beta\mathbb{I}) and (O¯​O¯†+β​𝕀)(\bar{O}\bar{O}^{\dagger}+\beta\mathbb{I}) are Hermitian positive definite matrices, which allow efficient inversion via Cholesky decomposition. However, these computations are prone to numerical instability in practice [2], necessitating double precision arithmetic for reliable computation.

An alternative approach is to apply the scaling factor mm to the O¯\bar{O} matrix by defining O~=mReO¯+iImO¯\tilde{O}=m\real\bar{O}+i\imaginary\bar{O}. While this leads to a similar formulation for SR δ​θ=(O~†​O~+β​𝕀)−1​O~†​ϵ¯\delta\theta=(\tilde{O}^{\dagger}\tilde{O}+\beta\mathbb{I})^{-1}\tilde{O}^{\dagger}\bar{\epsilon}, empirical results indicate that performance is improved by keeping the energy gradient O¯†​ϵ¯\bar{O}^{\dagger}\bar{\epsilon} unchanged. Consequently, we only use the modified matrix O~\tilde{O} in the preconditioning term. This results in the update rules of preconditioned gradient:

SR: δθ=(O~†O~+β𝕀)−1O¯†ϵ¯,\displaystyle\text{SR: }\delta\theta=(\tilde{O}^{\dagger}\tilde{O}+\beta\mathbb{I})^{-1}\bar{O}^{\dagger}\bar{\epsilon}, (22)
MinSR: δθ=O~†(O~O~†+β𝕀)−1(O~O~†+β𝕀)−1O~O¯†ϵ¯.\displaystyle\text{MinSR: }\delta\theta=\tilde{O}^{\dagger}(\tilde{O}\tilde{O}^{\dagger}+\beta\mathbb{I})^{-1}(\tilde{O}\tilde{O}^{\dagger}+\beta\mathbb{I})^{-1}\tilde{O}\bar{O}^{\dagger}\bar{\epsilon}. (23)

While this preconditioned approach lacks a physical interpretation as clear as the relative time-step approach derived above, it offers computational advantage as detailed in Section V. Further analysis for Eq. (22) and Eq. (23) are provided in the Supplementary Material. Finally, when the neural network parameters are real-valued but the outputs are complex, the O¯\bar{O} matrix and ϵ¯\bar{\epsilon} vector need to be replaced by stacking their real and imaginary parts along the first axis [52].

V Discussion

We benchmark our methods on the spin-1/2 J1−J2J_{1}-J_{2} Heisenberg model with first- and second-neighbor couplings,

H=J1​∑⟨i,j⟩si→⋅sj→+J2​∑⟨⟨i,j⟩⟩si→⋅sj→.H=J_{1}\sum_{\langle i,j\rangle}\vec{s_{i}}\cdot\vec{s_{j}}+J_{2}\sum_{\langle\langle i,j\rangle\rangle}\vec{s_{i}}\cdot\vec{s_{j}}. (24)

This model exhibits magnetic order at both small and large values of J2J_{2}, showing a Néel and a stripy pattern [54], respectively. Near the classical maximally frustrated point, J2/J1=0.5J_{2}/J_{1}=0.5, these orders vanish: current consensus is that this region is split into a ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} spin liquid and a valence-bond solid (VBS) [26, 55, 56]. We estimate the ground-state energy on a 6×66\times 6 square lattice with periodic boundary conditions at J2/J1=0J_{2}/J_{1}=0 (no frustration) and J2/J1=0.5J_{2}/J_{1}=0.5 (maximal frustration).

A square lattice is a bipartite graph whose points can be divided into two disjoint and independent sublattices, A and B, such that every interaction bond connects a point in sublattice A to one in sublattice B. In the J2=0J_{2}=0 limit, where only nearest-neighbor interactions exist, one sublattice is a checkerboard pattern. In the J1=0J_{1}=0 limit, where only next-nearest-neighbor interactions exist, a sublattice has a striped pattern consisting of alternating rows or columns. Under these two limits, the sign of the wave function for a spin configuration σ\sigma can be formally expressed as

sign​[ψ⁡(σ)]=(−1)MA​(σ),\text{sign}[\psi(\sigma)]=(-1)^{M_{A}(\sigma)}, (25)

where MAM_{A} represents the total number of up-spins in sublattice A for the configuration σ\sigma. This relation is known as the Marshall sign rule (MSR) [57]. While this rule does not hold exactly for arbitrary values of J1J_{1} and J2J_{2}, it serves as a good approximation for numerical calculations [58].

Figure 2 compares the energy learning curves for J2/J1=0J_{2}/J_{1}=0 and J2/J1=0.5J_{2}/J_{1}=0.5 using three different approaches: the original SR method with m=1m=1, our modified SR formulations (Eq. (20) and Eq. (22)), and our MinSR formulations (Eq. (21) and Eq. (23)). The choice of m=1m=1 proves problematic, as it causes rapid collapse of Monte Carlo samples into two checkerboard patterns with the smallest diagonal Hamiltonian element. This collapse leads to zero gradient norm and traps the energy in a local minimum. In contrast, both our modified SR and MinSR formulations successfully achieve state-of-the-art accuracy for both coupling ratios. The non-frustrated scenario has higher accuracy than the frustrated case. Note that the ϵ~\tilde{\epsilon} method converges slower due to our use of a smaller fixed learning rate rather than an adaptive one, which we implement for numerical stability. With extended training, all methods are expected to converge to comparable accuracy levels. Details of experimental setup are provided in the Supplementary Material.

The scaling factor mm requires some tuning: a value too small impedes phase convergence, while a value too large can induce training instability. We find that m=4m=4 and 1111 are effective for the modified ϵ~\tilde{\epsilon} [Eqs. (20)–(21)] and O~\tilde{O} [Eqs. (22)–(23)] methods, respectively. The optimal mm is likely system- and learning-rate-dependent. Furthermore, it would be of interest to develop criteria for automatically changing mm during the simulation along the ideas proposed in [2].

Having established the effectiveness of our approach, we now present quantitative analyses using the best-performing method–Eq. (22)–for both J2/J1=0J_{2}/J_{1}=0 and J2/J1=0.5J_{2}/J_{1}=0.5 cases. We compare ground state energies per site across different approaches. At J2/J1=0J_{2}/J_{1}=0, our work yields −0.6788-0.6788, showing excellent agreement with the exact value [59] of −0.678872-0.678872. At this coupling ratio, VMC method [60] gives −0.6785​(2)-0.6785(2), and CNN method [24] achieves −0.67882​(1)-0.67882(1). For J2/J1=0.5J_{2}/J_{1}=0.5, where the exact energy is −0.503810-0.503810, our calculation produces −0.5004-0.5004. The other methods produced the following results: VMC1 [61] obtained −0.50117​(1)-0.50117(1), VMC2 [60] reached −0.4985​(2)-0.4985(2), DMRG [62] achieved −0.503805-0.503805, and CNN [24] reported -0.50185(1).

Figure 3 shows the empirical cumulative distribution function for phase difference relative to MSR, ϕ−ϕM​S​R\phi-\phi_{MSR}, for J2/J1=0J_{2}/J_{1}=0 and J2/J1=0.5J_{2}/J_{1}=0.5. The cumulative distribution function of the random variable ϕ\phi evaluated at xx is the probability that ϕ−ϕM​S​R\phi-\phi_{MSR} takes a value less than or equal to xx, i.e., F⁡(x)=P​(ϕ−ϕM​S​R≤x)F(x)=\text{P}(\phi-\phi_{MSR}\leq x). Since two cases both have small standard deviations, our neural network with the improved stochastic reconfiguration method can effectively learn the Marshall sign rule.

For the frustrated case J2/J1=0.5J_{2}/J_{1}=0.5, we calculate the overlap of the true sign structure and the Marshall sign to estimate the deviation,

D=|∑σ|ψ0​(σ)|2​sign​[ψ0​(σ)]​M​(σ)|.D=\Bigg|\sum_{\sigma}|\psi_{0}(\sigma)|^{2}\text{sign}[\psi_{0}(\sigma)]\text{M}(\sigma)\Bigg|. (26)

where ψ0​(σ)\psi_{0}(\sigma) is the exact ground-state wave function from exact diagonalization, M​(σ)\text{M}(\sigma) is the Marshall sign for configuration σ\sigma. The overall absolute value is used to take into account the overall phase difference. According to the definition, 0≤D≤10\leq D\leq 1. If D=1D=1, then MSR is exactly true. If D<1D<1, the amount of difference from 1 indicates the total probability to have non-Marshall sign configurations. We find 49.76% symmetrized basis configurations having non-Marshall sign, but get D=0.9608D=0.9608. This shows that non-Marshall sign configurations have small amplitudes and hence contribute little to the Monte Carlo sampled energy gradient. We hypothesize that the simple architecture of the phase network adopted in this study is not capable of representing the non-Marshall sign configurations, which do not follow any known simple rules that could be learned by a few layers of perceptrons.

In summary, we propose an improved stochastic reconfiguration method that can efficiently train the phase and amplitude concurrently by employing a faster learning rate for the phase. While this study concentrates on a spin model, the methods are straightforward to generalize to other fermionic and non-stoquastic Hamiltonians (a Hamiltonian is called stoquastic with respect to a basis if every off-diagonal element in that basis is non-positive; conversely, the ground state of a non-stoquastic Hamiltonian exhibits both positive and negative amplitudes, which poses a challenge in learning the correct sign structure). Furthermore, our approach can be extended to larger system sizes and more complex NQS architectures. The optimization scheme may also prove valuable in the context of variational Monte Carlo calculations that do not employ NQS wave functions. Finally, we point out that the symmetry-adapted method proposed in Appendix A can be useful in more complicated cases where the ground state (or the state of interest) lies at a nonzero total wave vector 𝐤\mathbf{k} and complex symmetry.

Appendix A Symmetrized wave function

There are two main approaches to implementing space group symmetry in neural network wave functions. Let GG denote the space group with symmetry operations g^\hat{g}. The first step is to use data augmentation technique: we take each sampled state σ\sigma and generate symmetry-related spin configurations by applying group operations, g^​σ\hat{g}\sigma. The neural network is applied to all g^​σ\hat{g}\sigma separately, and the final result is taken as the average over this augmented symmetrized set. The same procedure is used for every initial state σ\sigma which we seek to find the value of ψθ​(σ)\psi_{\theta}(\sigma).

Alternatively, one can work with representative basis states. The idea is to pick a certain member σE\sigma_{E} of the symmetry-equivalent set g^​σ\hat{g}\sigma (OPENg^∈G)\hat{g}\in G) as a representative and use it as the input to the neural network for all member of the set. This amounts to fixing the symmetry gauge by mapping each spin configuration in the Monte Carlo sample to its representative spin configuration, and in this way the network never sees spin configurations other than the representatives.

The first method is commonly believed to be superior than using representative spin configuration [48] because this exposes the neural net to a wider variety of configurations and imposes physically relevant constraints on the network parameters. In the main text, we choose the data augmentation method. However, our numerical experiment shows that these two methods indeed have similar performance in the energy minimization process. Furthermore, the representative (”canonical”) configuration approach has advantages when the ground state is not of the completely symmetric 𝒌=0\bm{k}=0 type and the proper way of averaging of neural network outputs over the set g^​σ\hat{g}\sigma is not self-evident.

Using representative configurations for implementing the full space group symmetry in the lattice is a general method for any 𝒌\bm{k} point and any irreducible representation. The starting point is the equivalence class of a basis state σ\sigma, usually referred to as the orbit of σ\sigma, given by 𝒪(σ)={g^σ,∀g^∈G}\mathcal{O}(\sigma)=\{\hat{g}\sigma,\forall\hat{g}\in G\}. To distinguish between different orbits, we select a canonical configuration σE\sigma_{E} for each. An orbit forms a |𝒪||\mathcal{O}|-dimensional representation of GG, which is in general reducible. The normalized symmetrized basis states of an orbit are calculated by

|ϕm​tj​(σE)⟩=dj|G|​∑g∈GΓj​(g)m​t∗​|σg⟩,\ket{\phi_{mt}^j(\sigma_E)}=\sqrt{\frac{d_{j}}{|G|}}\sum_{g\in G}\Gamma^{j}(g)^{*}_{mt}\ket{\sigma_g}, (27)

where we use j≡(𝒌∗,β)j\equiv(\bm{{}^{*}k},\beta) as a collective index for the k-points 𝒌\bm{k} and irrep β\beta, dd is the dimension of the irrep, Γ\Gamma is the representation matrix, mm runs over all basis functions of the irrep, and tt represents the columns of Γ\Gamma. We can now write the wave function with the normalized symmetrized basis states

|Ψj⟩=∑σE,tΨj​(σE,t)​|ϕtj​(σE)⟩,\ket{\Psi^j}=\sum_{\sigma_{E},t}\Psi^{j}(\sigma_{E},t)\ket{\phi^j_t(\sigma_E)}, (28)

where the coefficients Ψj​(σE,t)\Psi^{j}(\sigma_{E},t) represent the wave function in the symmetrized basis.

The final step is to establish the link between the wave function in the symmetrized basis, |ϕtj​(σE)⟩\ket{\phi^j_t(\sigma_E)}, and the neural network output Ψnet​(σE)\Psi^{\text{net}}(\sigma_{E}). To obtain the coefficient Ψj​(σE,t)\Psi^{j}(\sigma_{E},t), we apply the method of inversion in which we select a subset G′⊂GG^{\prime}\subset G such that the matrix

Mg′​tj=dj|G|​Γj​(g′)1​t∗​ with ​g′∈G′M^{j}_{g^{\prime}t}=\sqrt{\frac{d_{j}}{|G|}}\Gamma^{j}(g^{\prime})^{*}_{1t}\text{ with }g^{\prime}\in G^{\prime} (29)

is invertible, and use Mg′​tjM^{j}_{g^{\prime}t} to calculate the coefficient as

Ψj​(σE,t)=∑g′∈G′[Mg′​tj]−1​Ψnet​(g^′​σE).\mathrm{\Psi}^{j}(\sigma_{E},t)=\sum_{g^{\prime}\in G^{\prime}}[M^{j}_{g^{\prime}t}]^{-1}\mathrm{\Psi}^{\text{net}}(\hat{g}^{\prime}\sigma_{E}). (30)

As Eq. (30) suggests, we parameterize the symmetrized wave function by the canonical basis state σE\sigma_{E}, the k-points, and irreps. Further details of this approach are given in the Supplementary Material.

For the Heisenberg J1−J2J_{1}-J_{2} model with J2/J1=0.5J_{2}/J_{1}=0.5, we compare the energy error per site using two different symmetrization approaches. The data augmentation method yields an energy error per site (Δ​E/N\Delta E/N) of 0.0034, while the representative method produces an error of 0.0049. These two errors are of the same order of magnitude, indicating comparable performance between two symmetrization methods.

1.1 Minimization of Eq. (12)

We start from the Lagrangian:

ℒMinSR′=β​∥δ​θ∥2+(δ​θ†​O¯†−ϵ¯†−Δ†)​μ+∥Δ∥2.\mathcal{L}_{\text{MinSR}}^{\prime}=\beta\lVert\delta\theta\rVert^{2}+(\delta\theta^{\dagger}\bar{O}^{\dagger}-\bar{\epsilon}^{\dagger}-\Delta^{\dagger})\mu+\lVert\Delta\rVert^{2}. (S1)

The optimality conditions are

∂ℒMinSR′∂(δ​θ†)=β​δ​θ+O¯†​μ=0\displaystyle\frac{\partial\mathcal{L}_{\text{MinSR}}^{\prime}}{\partial(\delta\theta^{\dagger})}=\beta\delta\theta+\bar{O}^{\dagger}\mu=0 (S2)
∂ℒMinSR′∂Δ†=−μ+Δ=0\displaystyle\frac{\partial\mathcal{L}_{\text{MinSR}}^{\prime}}{\partial\Delta^{\dagger}}=-\mu+\Delta=0 (S3)
∂ℒMinSR′∂μ=δ​θ†​O¯†−ϵ¯†−Δ†=0.\displaystyle\frac{\partial\mathcal{L}_{\text{MinSR}}^{\prime}}{\partial\mu}=\delta\theta^{\dagger}\bar{O}^{\dagger}-\bar{\epsilon}^{\dagger}-\Delta^{\dagger}=0. (S4)

We have two equations after eliminating Δ=μ\Delta=\mu

β​δ​θ+O¯†​μ=0\displaystyle\beta\delta\theta+\bar{O}^{\dagger}\mu=0 (S5)
O¯​δ​θ=ϵ¯+μ.\displaystyle\bar{O}\delta\theta=\bar{\epsilon}+\mu. (S6)

These two equations have two solutions. For the first solution, we start by obtaining δ​θ=−1β​O¯†​μ\delta\theta=-\frac{1}{\beta}\bar{O}^{\dagger}\mu from Eq. (S5). Then we substitute this expression of δ​θ\delta\theta into Eq. (S6), which gives μ=(−β)​(O¯​O¯†+β​𝕀)−1​ϵ¯\mu=(-\beta)(\bar{O}\bar{O}^{\dagger}+\beta\mathbb{I})^{-1}\bar{\epsilon}. Finally, replacing μ\mu in Eq. (S5) yields the first solution

δ​θ=O¯†​(O¯​O¯†+β​𝕀)−1​ϵ¯.\delta\theta=\bar{O}^{\dagger}(\bar{O}\bar{O}^{\dagger}+\beta\mathbb{I})^{-1}\bar{\epsilon}. (S7)

This is the same as the MinSR solution except adding the Tikhonov regularization to stabilize the inversion.

Alternatively, one can first multiply O¯†\bar{O}^{\dagger} from left on both sides of Eq. (S6) and make use of Eq. (S5) to obtain O¯†​O¯​δ​θ=O¯†​ϵ¯+O¯†​μ=O¯†​ϵ¯−β​δ​θ\bar{O}^{\dagger}\bar{O}\delta\theta=\bar{O}^{\dagger}\bar{\epsilon}+\bar{O}^{\dagger}\mu=\bar{O}^{\dagger}\bar{\epsilon}-\beta\delta\theta. Solving this equation yields the second solution

δ​θ=(O¯†​O¯+β​𝕀)−1​O¯†​ϵ¯,\delta\theta=(\bar{O}^{\dagger}\bar{O}+\beta\mathbb{I})^{-1}\bar{O}^{\dagger}\bar{\epsilon}, (S8)

which is the same as the SR solution with the Tikhonov regularization. The fact that both the SR and MinSR solutions can be derived from a single Lagrangian offers another way to see their mathematical equivalence.

ℒMinSRM=β​∥δ​θ∥2+(δ​θ†​O~†−ϵ¯′⁣†−Δ†)​μ+∥Δ∥2.\mathcal{L}_{\text{MinSR}}^{\text{M}}=\beta\lVert\delta\theta\rVert^{2}+(\delta\theta^{\dagger}\tilde{O}^{\dagger}-\bar{\epsilon}^{\prime\dagger}-\Delta^{\dagger})\mu+\lVert\Delta\rVert^{2}. (S16)

Adopting the MinSR-type solution δ​θ=O~†​(O~​O~†+β​𝕀)−1​ϵ¯′\delta\theta=\tilde{O}^{\dagger}(\tilde{O}\tilde{O}^{\dagger}+\beta\mathbb{I})^{-1}\bar{\epsilon}^{\prime} and substitute Eq. (S15), we obtain

δ​θ=O~†​(O~​O~†+β​𝕀)−1​(O~​O~†+β1​𝕀)−1​O~​O¯†​ϵ¯.\delta\theta=\tilde{O}^{\dagger}(\tilde{O}\tilde{O}^{\dagger}+\beta\mathbb{I})^{-1}(\tilde{O}\tilde{O}^{\dagger}+\beta_{1}\mathbb{I})^{-1}\tilde{O}\bar{O}^{\dagger}\bar{\epsilon}. (S17)

Alternatively, using the SVD decomposition, we can demonstrate the mathematical equivalence of the two preconditioned matrices,

(O~†​O~)−1=O~†​(O~​O~†)−1​(O~​O~†)−1​O~.(\tilde{O}^{\dagger}\tilde{O})^{-1}=\tilde{O}^{\dagger}(\tilde{O}\tilde{O}^{\dagger})^{-1}(\tilde{O}\tilde{O}^{\dagger})^{-1}\tilde{O}. (S18)

The regularization parameters β\beta and β1\beta_{1} are then added to ensure numerical stability. In practice, we set β\beta and β1\beta_{1} to be equal.

1.4 Nesterov’s accelerated gradient method

Nesterov’s accelerated gradient (NAG), a seminal advancement in optimization algorithms, has emerged as a cornerstone in the realm of machine learning and numerical optimization. NAG can be viewed as the discrete version of a second-order ordinary differential equation (ODE) [4],

d2θdt2+3t​dθdt+∇f​(θ)=0,\frac{\differential^{2}\theta}{\differential t^{2}}+\frac{3}{t}\frac{\differential\theta}{\differential t}+\nabla f(\theta)=0, (S19)

where the time parameter tt relates to the step size. This formulation reveals an intuitive physical interpretation: the optimization dynamics resemble a damped system. At small tt, the system is overdamped, smoothly converging to the equilibrium, while at larger tt, the system becomes underdamped, exhibiting oscillations with gradually diminishing amplitude.

Given an objective function f⁡(θ)f(\theta) to be minimized, the Nesterov’s accelerated gradient update [5] is given by

v→t+1\displaystyle\vec{v}_{t+1} =μv→t−ϵ∇f(θ→t+μv→t),\displaystyle=\mu\vec{v}_{t}-\epsilon\nabla f(\vec{\theta}_{t}+\mu\vec{v}_{t}), (S20)
θ→t+1\displaystyle\vec{\theta}_{t+1} =θ→t+v→t+1,\displaystyle=\vec{\theta}_{t}+\vec{v}_{t+1},

where ϵ>0\epsilon>0 is the learning rate, μ∈[0,1]\mu\in[0,1] is the momentum coefficient. θ→t\vec{\theta}_{t} and v→t\vec{v}_{t} are the parameter and momentum at optimization step tt, respectively. A key difference between NAG and classical momentum (CM) lies in the gradient evaluation: NAG computes ∇f​(θ→t+μ​v→t)\nabla f(\vec{\theta}_{t}+\mu\vec{v}_{t}), effectively ”looking ahead” in the momentum direction, whereas CM uses ∇f​(θ→t)\nabla f(\vec{\theta}_{t}) from the current position θt\theta_{t}. This subtle modification enhances NAG’s responsiveness, leading to more stable convergence, particularly for higher values of μ\mu [5].

Beyond direct application, alternative approaches have been proposed to integrate momentum methods into stochastic reconfiguration framework [2, 3]. These methods demonstrate the ability of momentum-based optimization in neural quantum states settings.

1.5 Adaptive learning rate

We also use an adaptive method to tune the learning rate, because convergence properties are strongly influenced by the choice of the learning rate: small values imply slow convergence rate, while large values may lead to oscillations or even divergence. The value of the learning rate is usually chosen by manual tuning and little attention has been paid to its automatic selection. Here, we propose to determine the learning rate for the subsequent step by maximizing the performance in the current step.

Suppose we have an objective function f⁡(θ→)f(\vec{\theta}), where θ→\vec{\theta} is the set of parameters. With updated parameters, this function will be f⁡(θ→+τ​η→)f(\vec{\theta}+\tau\vec{\eta}), where τ\tau is learning rate and η→\vec{\eta} is the search direction. We take first derivative to find the optimal learning rate τ0\tau_{0},

∂f∂τ|τ=τ0=η→⋅∇f|θ→+τ0​η→=0.\frac{\partial f}{\partial\tau}\Big|_{\tau=\tau_{0}}=\vec{\eta}\cdot\nabla f\Big|_{\vec{\theta}+\tau_{0}\vec{\eta}}=0. (S21)

In our current problem, the objective function f⁡(θ→)f(\vec{\theta}) is energy E⁡(θ→)E(\vec{\theta}), so that η→⋅∇E|θ→+τ0​η→=0\vec{\eta}\cdot\nabla E\Big|_{\vec{\theta}+\tau_{0}\vec{\eta}}=0. We define γ→=∇E\vec{\gamma}=\nabla E from now on.

After step nn, the values of γ→​(θ→)\vec{\gamma}(\vec{\theta}) and γ→​(θ→+τ(n)​η→)\vec{\gamma}(\vec{\theta}+\tau^{(n)}\vec{\eta}) are known, and we want to determine the optimal step size for the next iteration n+1n+1, satisfying γ→​(θ→+τ(n+1)​η→)⋅η→=0\vec{\gamma}(\vec{\theta}+\tau^{(n+1)\vec{\eta}})\cdot\vec{\eta}=0. This can be accomplished by linear interpolation,

γ→​(θ→)⋅η→+γ→​(θ→+τ(n)​η→)⋅η→−γ→​(θ→)⋅η→τ(n)​τ(n+1)=0.\vec{\gamma}(\vec{\theta})\cdot\vec{\eta}+\frac{\vec{\gamma}(\vec{\theta}+\tau^{(n)}\vec{\eta})\cdot\vec{\eta}-\vec{\gamma}(\vec{\theta})\cdot\vec{\eta}}{\tau^{(n)}}\tau^{(n+1)}=0. (S22)

Therefore, the recursion formula can be written as

τ(n+1)=τ(n)​γ→​(θ→)⋅η→γ→​(θ→)⋅η→−γ→​(θ→+τ(n)​η→)⋅η→.\tau^{(n+1)}=\tau^{(n)}\frac{\vec{\gamma}(\vec{\theta})\cdot\vec{\eta}}{\vec{\gamma}(\vec{\theta})\cdot\vec{\eta}-\vec{\gamma}(\vec{\theta}+\tau^{(n)}\vec{\eta})\cdot\vec{\eta}}. (S23)

In practice, γ→​(θ→+τ(n)​η→)\vec{\gamma}(\vec{\theta}+\tau^{(n)}\vec{\eta}) is estimated with updated wave function and local energies but with the old Monte Carlo sample. Notice that η→\vec{\eta} is not recalculated with updated neural network parameters. If 0<τ(n+1)<τ(n)0<\tau^{(n+1)}<\tau^{(n)}, the new learning rate is accepted; otherwise, we set τ(n+1)=min⁡(1.2​τ(n),0.2)\tau^{(n+1)}=\min(1.2\tau^{(n)},0.2) to prevent the learning rate from growing too fast.

Figure 1 compares energy learning curves with adaptive and fixed learning rate. Both Nesterov’s accelerated gradient method and adaptive learning rate speed up the energy minimization process in the initial stage. With adaptive learning rate, the choice of momentum value μ\mu doesn’t make much difference.

Table 1 and Table 2 summarize the experimental setups for the J2/J1=0J_{2}/J_{1}=0 and J2/J1=0.5J_{2}/J_{1}=0.5 cases, respectively. The methods referenced are defined as follows: the ϵ~\tilde{\epsilon} method by Eq. (20) and Eq. (21), the O~\tilde{O} method (SR) by Eq. (22), and the O~\tilde{O} method (MinSR) by Eq. (23) in the main text. 2 Space group symmetry

Here, we outline our approach to incorporate the full space group symmetry in the lattice using representative configuration. We first introduce the basic background of space group, and then describe how the symmetrized basis functions are obtained.

2.1 Background

Consider a space group 𝐆\bf{G} with a subgroup 𝐓=∑n{E|𝒕n}\bm{\mathrm{T}}=\sum_{n}\{E|\bm{t}_{n}\} of lattice translations written in the left coset decomposition,

𝐆={R1|𝝉1}​𝐓+{R2|𝝉2}​𝐓+…+{Rh|𝝉h}​𝐓,\bm{\mathrm{G}}=\{R_{1}|\bm{\tau}_{1}\}\bm{\mathrm{T}}+\{R_{2}|\bm{\tau}_{2}\}\bm{\mathrm{T}}+...+\{R_{h}|\bm{\tau}_{h}\}\bm{\mathrm{T}}, (S24)

where RjR_{j} are point operations and 𝝉j\bm{\tau}_{j} are fractional translations of least possible magnitude associated with RjR_{j}. In non-symmorphic space groups, the left coset representatives {Rj|𝝉j}\{R_{j}|\bm{\tau}_{j}\} themselves do not generally form a group, but the factor group 𝐆/𝐓\bf{G}/\bf{T} is isomorphic with the point group 𝐅\bf{F} formed by hh elements RjR_{j}. The latter is called the isogonal point group of 𝐆\bf{G} and plays a key role in determining the symmetries of Bloch wave vectors and hence in classifying space group representations.

In fermionic systems, a basis function x can be expressed as a Slater determinant:

xL​(r1,r2,…,rN,s1,s2,…,sN)=1N!​|ϕl1σ1​(r1,s1)ϕl1σ1​(r2,s2)...ϕl1σ1​(rN,sN)ϕl2σ2​(r1,s1)ϕl2σ2​(r2,s2)...ϕl2σ2​(rN,sN)............ϕlNσN​(r1,s1)ϕlNσN​(r2,s2)...ϕlNσN​(rN,sN)|,\textbf{x}_{L}(r_{1},r_{2},...,r_{N};s_{1},s_{2},...,s_{N})=\frac{1}{\sqrt{N!}}\begin{vmatrix}\phi_{l_{1}}^{\sigma_{1}}(r_{1},s_{1})&\phi_{l_{1}}^{\sigma_{1}}(r_{2},s_{2})&...&\phi_{l_{1}}^{\sigma_{1}}(r_{N},s_{N})\\ \phi_{l_{2}}^{\sigma_{2}}(r_{1},s_{1})&\phi_{l_{2}}^{\sigma_{2}}(r_{2},s_{2})&...&\phi_{l_{2}}^{\sigma_{2}}(r_{N},s_{N})\\ ...&...&...&...\\ \phi_{l_{N}}^{\sigma_{N}}(r_{1},s_{1})&\phi_{l_{N}}^{\sigma_{N}}(r_{2},s_{2})&...&\phi_{l_{N}}^{\sigma_{N}}(r_{N},s_{N})\end{vmatrix}, (S25)

where L={l1,l2,…,lN;σ1,σ2,…,σN}L=\{l_{1},l_{2},...,l_{N};\sigma_{1},\sigma_{2},...,\sigma_{N}\} denotes the orbit label (site ll and spin σ\sigma), ϕliσi​(rj)=ϕiσ​(rj−li)\phi_{l_{i}}^{\sigma_{i}}(r_{j})=\phi^{\sigma}_{i}(r_{j}-l_{i}) is the spatial orbital, NN is the total number of electrons, (rir_{i}, sis_{i}) represents the electron coordinate and spin. This formulation naturally extends to spin systems, which form a subset of fermionic models with a constraint that each site is occupied by one electron. In this case, the allowed moves must involve an even number of fermionic permutations (e.g., two-electrons exchanges). Consequently, the permutation signs are always +1+1, effectively resulting in Bose statistics.

A space group operation g^={R|𝝉+𝒕}\hat{g}=\{R|\bm{\tau}+\bm{t}\} acts on x as

g^​xL=1N!​|g​ϕl1σ1​(r1,s1)g​ϕl1σ1​(r2,s2)...g​ϕl1σ1​(rN,sN)g​ϕl2σ2​(r1,s1)g​ϕl2σ2​(r2,s2)...g​ϕl2σ2​(rN,sN)............g​ϕlNσN​(r1,s1)g​ϕlNσN​(r2,s2)...g​ϕlNσN​(rN,sN)|=(−1)Pg​x′.\hat{g}\textbf{x}_{L}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{N!}}\begin{vmatrix}g\phi_{l_{1}}^{\sigma_{1}}(r_{1},s_{1})&g\phi_{l_{1}}^{\sigma_{1}}(r_{2},s_{2})&...&g\phi_{l_{1}}^{\sigma_{1}}(r_{N},s_{N})\\ g\phi_{l_{2}}^{\sigma_{2}}(r_{1},s_{1})&g\phi_{l_{2}}^{\sigma_{2}}(r_{2},s_{2})&...&g\phi_{l_{2}}^{\sigma_{2}}(r_{N},s_{N})\\ ...&...&...&...\\ g\phi_{l_{N}}^{\sigma_{N}}(r_{1},s_{1})&g\phi_{l_{N}}^{\sigma_{N}}(r_{2},s_{2})&...&g\phi_{l_{N}}^{\sigma_{N}}(r_{N},s_{N})\end{vmatrix}=(-1)^{P_{g}}\textbf{x}^{\prime}. (S26)

g^\hat{g} transforms x into another basis function x′\textbf{x}^{\prime} by permuting the rows of the determinant, and PgP_{g} denotes the number of permutations performed. For consistency, we must define a ’canonical order’ that specifies how each row should be permuted. For example, in Equation (S25) the rows are permuted along lil_{i}; for the same lil_{i}, spin ↓\downarrow comes before spin ↑\uparrow. The canonical order can be chosen in various ways so long as the ordering is consistent throughout the calculations.

We adopt an ”active” convention for symmetry transformations. The transformation of the basis states works as follows:

g^​|x⟩=|g^​x⟩,\hat{g}\ket{\textbf{x}}=\ket{\hat{g}\textbf{x}}, (S27)

and the operator g^\hat{g} transforms an arbitrary many-body state |Ψ⟩=∑xΨ⁡(x)​|x⟩\ket{\mathrm{\Psi}}=\sum_{x}\mathrm{\Psi}(\textbf{x})\ket{\textbf{x}} as

g^​|Ψ⟩=∑xΨ⁡(x)​|g^​x⟩=∑xΨ⁡(g^−1​x)​|x⟩.\hat{g}\ket{\mathrm{\Psi}}=\sum_{x}\mathrm{\Psi}(\textbf{x})\ket{\hat{g}\textbf{x}}=\sum_{x}\mathrm{\Psi}(\hat{g}^{-1}\textbf{x})\ket{\textbf{x}}. (S28)

As Equation (S28) shows, to obtain g^​|Ψ⟩\hat{g}\ket{\mathrm{\Psi}} one can either transform the basis states |x⟩\ket{\textbf{x}} with fixed coefficients Ψ⁡(x)\mathrm{\Psi}(\textbf{x}), or transform the coefficient array.

The Bloch theorem for a single-particle state is written as

{E|𝒕}ψ𝐤(𝒓0)=ψ𝐤(𝒓0−𝒕)=e−i𝐤⋅𝐭ψ𝐤(𝒓0),\{E|\bm{t}\}\psi_{\bf{k}}(\bm{r}_{0})=\psi_{\bf{k}}(\bm{r}_{0}-\bm{t})=e^{-i\bf{k}\cdot\bm{t}}\psi_{\bf{k}}(\bm{r}_{0}), (S29)

and for the many-body state, we have

{E|𝒕}Ψ𝐤(x)=e−i𝒌⋅𝒕Ψ𝐤(x).\{E|\bm{t}\}\mathrm{\Psi}_{\bf{k}}(\textbf{x})=e^{-i\bm{k}\cdot\bm{t}}\mathrm{\Psi}_{\bf{k}}(\textbf{x}). (S30)

Equations (S29) and (S30) show that the representations of 𝐓\bm{\mathrm{T}} are one-dimensional and labeled by the wave vector 𝐤\bf{k} from the first Brillouin zone (1BZ).

Applying a symmetry element {S|𝒘}\{S|\bm{w}\} to a many-body Bloch function at wave vector 𝐤\bf{k} gives a Bloch function at wave vector S​𝐤S\bf{k} (see Sec. 3.6 in [1]):

{S|𝒘}​Ψ𝐤​(x)=ΨS​𝐤​({S|𝒘}−1​x).\{S|\bm{w}\}\mathrm{\Psi}_{\bf{k}}(\textbf{x})=\mathrm{\Psi}_{S\bf{k}}(\{S|\bm{w}\}^{-1}\textbf{x}). (S31)

Now, suppose that 𝚪\bf{\Gamma} is a representation of 𝐆\bf{G}; then the elements in 𝚪\bf{\Gamma} that represent translations form a representation of 𝐓\bf{T}, which in general is reducible. Suppose that it reduces to representations characterized by wave vectors 𝐤𝟏,𝐤𝟐,…,𝐤𝐝\bf{k}_{1},\bf{k}_{2},...,\bf{k}_{d}. As shown by Equation (S30), there exists a basis that consists of Bloch functions characterized by 𝐤𝟏,𝐤𝟐,…,𝐤𝐝\bf{k}_{1},\bf{k}_{2},...,\bf{k}_{d}. Since these Bloch functions are eigenstates of 𝐓\bf{T}, in this basis the elements of 𝐓\bf{T} are represented by diagonal matrices with diagonal elements given by e−i​𝐤𝐩​𝐭e^{-i\bf{k_{p}t}} (p = 1 to d).

Equation (S31) implies we can obtain 𝐤𝟏,𝐤𝟐,…,𝐤𝐝\bf{k}_{1},\bf{k}_{2},...,\bf{k}_{d} by applying point group operations RR from the isogonal point group 𝐅\bf{F}. For some vector 𝐤𝟏∈\bf{k}_{1}\in 1BZ, we define the 𝑠𝑡𝑎𝑟\it{star} of 𝐤𝟏\bf{k}_{1} to be a set of distinct wave vectors obtained by applying point group operations:

∗k=𝐤𝟏,𝐤𝟐,…,𝐤𝐪=⋃R∈𝐅R𝐤𝟏.{}^{*}\textbf{k}={\bf{k}_{1},\bf{k}_{2},...,\bf{k}_{q}}=\bigcup_{R\in\bf{F}}R\bf{k_{1}}. (S32)

Two wave vectors that differ by a reciprocal lattice vector 𝐠\bf{g} are considered equivalent, and we write R​𝐤𝟏≡𝐤𝟏R\bf{k_{1}}\equiv\bf{k_{1}} if R​𝐤𝟏=𝐤𝟏+𝐠R\bf{k_{1}}=\bf{k_{1}}+\bf{g}.

The little co-group of 𝐤𝟏\bf{k_{1}} consists of those operations S∈𝐅S\in\bf{F} which leave 𝐤𝟏\bf{k_{1}} invariant or transforms it into an equivalent vector, i.e. S​𝐤𝟏≡𝐤𝟏S\bf{k_{1}}\equiv\bf{k_{1}}. We denote this subgroup of 𝐅\bf{F} by 𝐆¯𝐤𝟏\bar{\bf{G}}^{\bf{}_{k_{1}}}. If Q​𝐤𝟏=𝐤𝟐Q\bf{k_{1}}=\bf{k_{2}} is another member of the star then we have

𝐆¯𝐤𝟐=Q​𝐆¯𝐤𝟏​Q−1,\bar{\bf{G}}^{\bf{k}_{2}}=Q\bar{\bf{G}}^{\bf{k}_{1}}Q^{-1}, (S33)

i.e., little co-groups at 𝐤𝟏,𝐤𝟐,…,𝐤𝐪\bf{k_{1}},\bf{k_{2}},...,\bf{k_{q}} form a set of conjugate subgroups of 𝐅\bf{F}. Furthermore, the group 𝐅\bf{F} can be expressed as a sum of left cosets with respect to 𝐆¯𝐤𝟏\bar{\bf{G}}^{\bf{k}_{1}}:

F=E​𝐆¯𝐤𝟏+Q2​𝐆¯𝐤𝟏+…+Qq​𝐆¯𝐤𝟏,\textbf{F}=E\bar{\bf{G}}^{\bf{k}_{1}}+Q_{2}\bar{\bf{G}}^{\bf{k}_{1}}+...+Q_{q}\bar{\bf{G}}^{\bf{k}_{1}}, (S34)

where 𝐤𝐢=𝐐𝐢​𝐤𝟏\bf{k_{i}}=Q_{i}\bf{k_{1}} and we have made the explicit choice Q1=EQ_{1}=E. These relations will be useful for constructing representations of the full space group 𝐆\bf{G}.

Next we introduce the little group 𝐆𝐤𝟏\bf{G}^{\bf{k}_{1}}, which is a space group obtained as a subgroup of 𝐆\bf{G} in Equation (S24) formed by left cosets with the rotational parts E,S2,…,SbE,S_{2},...,S_{b} from the little co-group 𝐆¯𝐤𝟏\bar{\bf{G}}^{\bf{k}_{1}}:

G𝐤𝟏={E|𝝉1}​T+{S2|𝝉2}​T+…+{Sb|𝝉b}​T.\textbf{G}^{\bf{k}_{1}}=\{E|\bm{\tau}_{1}\}\textbf{T}+\{S_{2}|\bm{\tau}_{2}\}\textbf{T}+...+\{S_{b}|\bm{\tau}_{b}\}\textbf{T}. (S35)

Essentially, 𝐆𝐤𝟏\bf{G}^{\bf{k}_{1}} is the space group containing all symmetry operations of wave vector 𝐤𝟏\bf{k_{1}}. We can then express the full space group as a sum of left cosets with respect to the little groups 𝐆𝐤𝟏\bf{G}^{\bf{k}_{1}}:

G={Q1|𝜻1}​G𝐤𝟏+{Q2|𝜻2}​G𝐤𝟏+…+{Qq|𝜻q}​G𝐤𝟏.\textbf{G}=\{Q_{1}|\bm{\zeta}_{1}\}\textbf{G}^{\bf{k}_{1}}+\{Q_{2}|\bm{\zeta}_{2}\}\textbf{G}^{\bf{k}_{1}}+...+\{Q_{q}|\bm{\zeta}_{q}\}\textbf{G}^{\bf{k}_{1}}. (S36)

A small representation 𝚪β𝐤𝟏\mathbf{\Gamma}_{\beta}^{\bf{k_{1}}} of G𝐤𝟏\textbf{G}^{\bf{k}_{1}} is an irreducible representation of G𝐤𝟏\textbf{G}^{\bf{k}_{1}} whose basis functions satisfy the Bloch theorem in Equation (S29) and (S30). Let the basis functions of 𝚪β𝐤𝟏\mathbf{\Gamma}_{\beta}^{\bf{k_{1}}} with dimensionality rr be written as

Ψ𝐤𝟏,𝟏β​(x),Ψ𝐤𝟏,𝟐β​(x),…,Ψ𝐤𝟏,𝐫β​(x).\mathrm{\Psi}_{\bf{k_{1}},1}^{\beta}(x),\mathrm{\Psi}_{\bf{k_{1}},2}^{\beta}(x),...,\mathrm{\Psi}_{\bf{k_{1}},r}^{\beta}(x). (S37)

Then we can obtain an irreducible representation of the space group 𝐆\bf{G} by forming a linear closure of the vector space spanned by the functions

{Qj|𝜻j}​Ψ𝐤𝟏,𝐢β​(x),\{Q_{j}|\bm{\zeta}_{j}\}\mathrm{\Psi}_{\bf{k_{1}},i}^{\beta}(x), (S38)

where j=1 to ​qj=\text{1 to }q, i=1 to ​ri=\text{1 to }r, and {Qj|𝜻j}\{Q_{j}|\bm{\zeta}_{j}\} is any set of left coset representatives from Equation (S36). The dimension of this representation is d=q​r=h​r/bd=qr=hr/b.

This reduces the task of finding representations of 𝐆\bf{G} to the simpler task of finding small representations of 𝐆𝐤\bf{G}^{\bf{k}} for all 𝐤\bf{k} in the first Brillouin zone. The matrices of small representations of 𝐆𝐤\bf{G}^{\bf{k}} have the following simple form:

𝚪β𝐤({R|𝐯})=e−i𝐤⋅𝐯𝐃β𝐤(R),\mathbf{\Gamma}_{\beta}^{\mathbf{k}}(\{R|\mathbf{v}\})=e^{-i\mathbf{k\cdot v}}\mathbf{D}_{\beta}^{\bf{k}}(R), (S39)

where 𝐯=𝝉+𝒕\mathbf{v}=\bm{\tau}+\bm{t} and 𝐃β𝐤​(R)\mathbf{D}_{\beta}^{\bf{k}}(R) are the same for all left cosets in Equation (S35). 𝐃β𝐤​(R)\mathbf{D}_{\beta}^{\bf{k}}(R) can be calculated with the method of projective representations [1], and they obey the following product rule:

𝐃β𝐤(Ri)𝐃β𝐤(Rj)=e−i𝒈i⋅𝝉j𝐃β𝐤(RiRj),\mathbf{D}_{\beta}^{\bf{k}}(R_{i})\mathbf{D}_{\beta}^{\bf{k}}(R_{j})=e^{-i\bm{g}_{i}\cdot\bm{\tau}_{j}}\mathbf{D}_{\beta}^{\bf{k}}(R_{i}R_{j}), (S40)

where 𝝉j\bm{\tau}_{j} is the fractional translation associated with RjR_{j} and 𝒈i=Ri−1​𝐤−𝐤\bm{g}_{i}=R_{i}^{-1}\bf{k}-\bf{k}.

2.2 Symmetrized Supercell Basis

In order to study physical models in reality, we construct supercells with lattice vectors that consist of primitive lattice vectors:

Ai=∑jMi​j​aj,\textbf{A}_{i}=\sum_{j}\textbf{M}_{ij}\textbf{a}_{j}, (S41)

where Ai\textbf{A}_{i} denotes the supercell lattice vectors, Mi​j\textbf{M}_{ij} is a matrix of integers, and aj\textbf{a}_{j} represents primitive lattice vectors. We use tn\textbf{t}_{n} to denote the lattice vectors pointing to lattice sites n=n= 1,…,NsN_{s}, where NS=|M|N_{S}=|\textbf{M}| is the number of lattice sites. The translations tn\textbf{t}_{n} form a finite group TS\textbf{T}_{S} under periodic boundary conditions. Let GS\textbf{G}_{S} denote the symmetry group of the supercell with symmetry operations gn^={R|𝝉+tn}\hat{g_{n}}=\{R|\bm{\tau}+\textbf{t}_{n}\}, which transforms the supercell sites into themselves.

Let x denote the normalized unsymmetrized basis states, we define the orbit of x to be

𝒪⁡(x)=⋃gn∈GSgn^​x.\mathcal{O}(\textbf{x})=\bigcup_{g_{n}\in\textbf{G}_{S}}\hat{g_{n}}\textbf{x}. (S42)

𝒪⁡(x)\mathcal{O}(\textbf{x}) is the set of all distinct basis states that can be obtained by applying space group operations to x. The orbit is closed under GS\textbf{G}_{S}: any symmetry operation in GS\textbf{G}_{S} would bring an element x∈𝒪\textbf{x}\in\mathcal{O} to another element x′∈𝒪\textbf{x}^{\prime}\in\mathcal{O}. The set of all basis states can then be constructed by non-overlapping orbits. To distinguish between different orbits, we chose a ”canonical” basis state xE\textbf{x}_{E} in each orbit as a reference. xE\textbf{x}_{E} can be defined arbitrarily as long as the definition is consistent and reproducible for all orbits. In practice, basis states are represented by arrays of integers. One way to define xE\textbf{x}_{E} is to sort the basis states in the orbit and choose the nth state. We can now use xE\textbf{x}_{E} to express other states in 𝒪⁡(x)\mathcal{O}(\textbf{x}) as

xgn=g^n​xE.\textbf{x}_{g_{n}}=\hat{g}_{n}\textbf{x}_{E}. (S43)

In this way, the basis states as well as their wave functions are related in an orbit, which reduces the number of unique wave function values by a factor of |𝒪||\mathcal{O}|. The network now requires less trainable parameters to approximate the wave functions and thus improving the efficiency of network training.

2.2.1 Symmetrized Wave Function

An orbit forms a |𝒪||\mathcal{O}|-dimensional representation of GS\textbf{G}_{S} which is reducible in general. In order to utilize the symmetry properties of the wave functions, we express the normalized symmetrized basis functions of the orbit as

|ϕm​tj​(xE)⟩=dj|GS|​∑g∈GS𝚪j​(g)m​t∗​|xg⟩,\ket{\phi_{mt}^j(\textbf{x}_E)}=\sqrt{\frac{d_{j}}{|\textbf{G}_{S}|}}\sum_{g\in\textbf{G}_{S}}\mathbf{\Gamma}^{j}(g)^{*}_{mt}\ket{\textbf{x}_g}, (S44)

where we use j≡(*k,β)j\equiv(\textbf{*k},\beta) as a collective index for the k-points k and irrep β\beta, dd is the dimension of the irrep, 𝚪\mathbf{\Gamma} is the irrep matrix defined in Equation (S39), mm runs over all basis functions of the irrep, and tt represents the columns of 𝚪\mathbf{\Gamma}. We can now write the wave function with the normalized symmetrized basis states:

|Ψj⟩=∑xE,tΨj​(xE,t)​|ϕtj​(xE)⟩.\ket{\mathrm{\Psi}^j}=\sum_{\textbf{x}_{E},t}\mathrm{\Psi}^{j}(\textbf{x}_{E},t)\ket{\phi^j_{t}(\textbf{x}_E)}. (S45)

Substituting Equation (S44) into (S45), a general state can be expressed as

|Ψj⟩=∑xE,tΨj​(xE,t)​dj|GS|​∑g∈GS𝚪j​(g)1​t∗​|xg⟩=∑xE,g∈GS(∑tΨj​(xE,t)​dj|GS|​𝚪j​(g)1​t∗)​|xg⟩=∑xE,g∈GSΨnet​(xE,g)​|xg⟩,\displaystyle\begin{split}\ket{\mathrm{\Psi}^j}&=\sum_{\textbf{x}_{E},t}\mathrm{\Psi}^{j}(\textbf{x}_{E},t)\sqrt{\frac{d_{j}}{|\textbf{G}_{S}|}}\sum_{g\in\textbf{G}_{S}}\mathbf{\Gamma}^{j}(g)^{*}_{1t}\ket{\textbf{x}_g}\\ &=\sum_{\textbf{x}_{E},g\in\textbf{G}_{S}}\left(\sum_{t}\mathrm{\Psi}^{j}(\textbf{x}_{E},t)\sqrt{\frac{d_{j}}{|\textbf{G}_{S}|}}\mathbf{\Gamma}^{j}(g)^{*}_{1t}\right)\ket{\textbf{x}_g}\\ &=\sum_{\textbf{x}_{E},g\in\textbf{G}_{S}}\mathrm{\Psi}^{\text{net}}(\textbf{x}_{E},g)\ket{\textbf{x}_g},\end{split} (S46)

where we select m=1m=1, and expression in the parenthesis can be represented by the network representation of the wave function Ψnet​(xg)\mathrm{\Psi}^{\text{net}}(\textbf{x}_{g}). The coefficient Ψj​(xE,t)\mathrm{\Psi}^{j}(\textbf{x}_{E},t) can be obtained by method of ”inversion”, where we select a subset GS′⊂GS\textbf{G}_{S}^{\prime}\subset\textbf{G}_{S} such that the matrix

Mg′​tj=dj|GS|​𝚪j​(g′)1​t∗​ with ​g′∈GS′\textbf{M}^{j}_{g^{\prime}t}=\sqrt{\frac{d_{j}}{|\textbf{G}_{S}|}}\mathbf{\Gamma}^{j}(g^{\prime})^{*}_{1t}\text{ with }g^{\prime}\in\textbf{G}_{S}^{\prime} (S47)

is invertible, and use Mg′​tj\textbf{M}^{j}_{g^{\prime}t} to calculate

Ψj​(xE,t)=∑g′∈GS′[Mj]g′​t−1​Ψnet​(g^′​xE).\mathrm{\Psi}^{j}(\textbf{x}_{E},t)=\sum_{g^{\prime}\in\textbf{G}_{S}^{\prime}}[\textbf{M}^{j}]^{-1}_{g^{\prime}t}\mathrm{\Psi}^{\text{net}}(\hat{g}^{\prime}\textbf{x}_{E}). (S48)

Therefore, we can express any quantum state in the normalized symmetrized basis states with the symmetrized wave functions, which brings a great reduction in the dimension of the Hilbert space.

2.2.2 Symmetrized Energy, Loss and Gradient

Given the symmetrized wave function in Equation (S46), we can write the symmetrized average energy as

Ej=∑{xE,t}∈SE≠wj​(xE,t)​Ej​(xE,t),E^{j}=\sum_{\{\textbf{x}_{E},t\}\in\textbf{S}_{E\neq}}w^{j}(\textbf{x}_{E},t)E^{j}(\textbf{x}_{E},t), (S49)

where SE≠\textbf{S}_{E\neq} is the set of unique canonical basis states, wj​(xE,t)w^{j}(\textbf{x}_{E},t) is the normalized weight which approximates the probability of the basis state (xE,t)(\textbf{x}_{E},t), and Ej​(xE,t)E^{j}(\textbf{x}_{E},t) denotes the local energy at state (xE,t)(\textbf{x}_{E},t). The normalized weights can be approximated by

wj​(xE,t)=|Ψj​(xE,t)|2∑{xE′,t′}∈SE≠|Ψj​(xE′,t′)|2.w^{j}(\textbf{x}_{E},t)=\frac{|\mathrm{\Psi}^{j}(\textbf{x}_{E},t)|^{2}}{\sum_{\{\textbf{x}_{E}^{\prime},t^{\prime}\}\in\textbf{S}_{E\neq}}|\mathrm{\Psi}^{j}(\textbf{x}_{E}^{\prime},t^{\prime})|^{2}}. (S50)

The local energy is given by

Ej​(xE,t)=Ψj​(xE,t)−1​∑yE∑s=1nyEjHt​sj​(xE,yE)​Ψj​(yE,s),E^{j}(\textbf{x}_{E},t)=\mathrm{\Psi}^{j}(\textbf{x}_{E},t)^{-1}\sum_{\textbf{y}_{E}}\sum_{s=1}^{n_{\textbf{y}_{E}}^{j}}H_{ts}^{j}(\textbf{x}_{E},\textbf{y}_{E})\mathrm{\Psi}^{j}(\textbf{y}_{E},s), (S51)

where the Hamiltonian Ht​sjH_{ts}^{j} and states yE\textbf{y}_{E} are described in detail in the next subsection.

The gradient of the average energy is modified to

∂wEj≈2​∑{xE,t}∈SE≠wj​(xE,t)​Re​[(Ej​(xE,t)−Ej)​Ψj​(xE,t)​∂wΨj​(xE,t)∗],\partial_{w}E^{j}\approx 2\sum_{\{\textbf{x}_{E},t\}\in\textbf{S}_{E\neq}}w^{j}(\textbf{x}_{E},t)\text{Re}[(E^{j}(\textbf{x}_{E},t)-E^{j})\mathrm{\Psi}^{j}(\textbf{x}_{E},t)\partial_{w}\mathrm{\Psi}^{j}(\textbf{x}_{E},t)^{*}], (S52)

and the loss function is defined to be

Lj=∑{xE′,t′}∈SE≠gj​(xE,t)​Ψj​(xE,t)∗.L^{j}=\sum_{\{\textbf{x}_{E}^{\prime},t^{\prime}\}\in\textbf{S}_{E\neq}}g^{j}(\textbf{x}_{E},t)\mathrm{\Psi}^{j}(\textbf{x}_{E},t)^{*}. (S53)

where gj​(xE,t)=2​wj​(xE,t)​Re​[(Ej​(xE,t)−Ej)​Ψj​(xE,t)]g^{j}(\textbf{x}_{E},t)=2w^{j}(\textbf{x}_{E},t)\text{Re}[(E^{j}(\textbf{x}_{E},t)-E^{j})\mathrm{\Psi}^{j}(\textbf{x}_{E},t)].

The main difference is that now the network manages to find the lowest energy state with respect to a specific k-point and irrep.

2.2.3 Symmetrized Hamiltonian

To calculate the local energy in Equation (S51), we need to obtain the Hamiltonian matrix Ht​sjH_{ts}^{j} and states yE\textbf{y}_{E} for a given canonical states xE\textbf{x}_{E}. Let a general Hamiltonian matrix element be expressed as

⟨ϕm​tj​(xE)|​H^​|ϕn​si​(yE)⟩=di​dj|GS|2​∑g,h𝚪j​(g)m​t​𝚪i​(h)n​s∗​⟨g^​xE|H^|h^​yE⟩=di​dj|GS|2​∑g,h𝚪j​(g)m​t​𝚪i​(g​h)n​s∗​⟨xE|H^|h^​yE⟩.\displaystyle\begin{split}\bra{\phi_{mt}^j(x_E)}\hat{H}\ket{\phi_{ns}^i(y_E)}&=\sqrt{\frac{d_{i}d_{j}}{|\textbf{G}_{S}|^{2}}}\sum_{g,h}\mathbf{\Gamma}^{j}(g)_{mt}\mathbf{\Gamma}^{i}(h)^{*}_{ns}\matrixelement{\hat{g}x_E}{\hat{H}}{\hat{h}y_E}\\ &=\sqrt{\frac{d_{i}d_{j}}{|\textbf{G}_{S}|^{2}}}\sum_{g,h}\mathbf{\Gamma}^{j}(g)_{mt}\mathbf{\Gamma}^{i}(gh)^{*}_{ns}\matrixelement{x_E}{\hat{H}}{\hat{h}y_E}.\end{split} (S54)

The second line is obtained by rewriting the matrix element as ⟨g^​xE|H^|h^​yE⟩=⟨xE|g^−1​H^​g^|g^−1​h^​yE⟩=⟨xE|H^|g^−1​h^​yE⟩\matrixelement{\hat{g}x_E}{\hat{H}}{\hat{h}y_E}=\matrixelement{x_E}{\hat{g}^{-1}\hat{H}\hat{g}}{\hat{g}^{-1}\hat{h}y_E}=\matrixelement{x_E}{\hat{H}}{\hat{g}^{-1}\hat{h}y_E}, and substituting g^−1​h^⇒h^\hat{g}^{-1}\hat{h}\Rightarrow\hat{h}.

We can expand 𝚪i​(g​h)∗\mathbf{\Gamma}^{i}(gh)^{*} into a matrix product of 𝚪i​(g)∗\mathbf{\Gamma}^{i}(g)^{*} and 𝚪i​(h)∗\mathbf{\Gamma}^{i}(h)^{*} to get

⟨ϕm​tj​(xE)|​H^​|ϕn​si​(yE)⟩=di​dj|GS|2​∑p∑g,h𝚪j​(g)m​t​𝚪i​(g)n​p∗​𝚪i​(h)p​s∗​⟨xE|H^|h^​yE⟩=δi​j​δm​n​∑h𝚪i​(h)t​s∗​⟨xE|H^|h^​yE⟩=|GS|di​δi​j​δm​n​⟨xE|H^|ϕt​sj​(yE)⟩.\displaystyle\begin{split}\bra{\phi_{mt}^j(x_E)}\hat{H}\ket{\phi_{ns}^i(y_E)}&=\sqrt{\frac{d_{i}d_{j}}{|\textbf{G}_{S}|^{2}}}\sum_{p}\sum_{g,h}\mathbf{\Gamma}^{j}(g)_{mt}\mathbf{\Gamma}^{i}(g)^{*}_{np}\mathbf{\Gamma}^{i}(h)^{*}_{ps}\matrixelement{x_E}{\hat{H}}{\hat{h}y_E}\\ &=\delta^{ij}\delta_{mn}\sum_{h}\mathbf{\Gamma}^{i}(h)^{*}_{ts}\matrixelement{x_E}{\hat{H}}{\hat{h}y_E}\\ &=\sqrt{\frac{|\textbf{G}_{S}|}{d_{i}}}\delta^{ij}\delta_{mn}\matrixelement{x_E}{\hat{H}}{\phi_{ts}^j(y_E)}.\end{split} (S55)

The result indicates that the Hamiltonian becomes block-diagonal with blocks indexed by j≡(k∗,β)j\equiv(\textbf{k}^{*},\beta) and irrep row indices mm. Each block has matrix elements indexed by orbit states (xE,yE)(x_{E},y_{E}) and irrep basis sets (s,t)(s,t). The steps to calculate the symmetrized Hamiltonian are described in Algorithm 1.
